title: Fluorescence, atomic spectra and emission/absorption line spectra
sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf
paragraphs: When an atomic gas or vapours kept at less than atmospheric pressure is suitably excited, the emitted radiation has a spectrum which contains certain specific wavelengths only.
For your information — FLUORESCENCE

Objects glow in the visible spectrum when illuminated by an ultraviolet light. Emissions are characteristic of the mineral involved, since they are related to its energy levels. In the case of scorpions, proteins near the surface of their skin give off the characteristic blue glow.
This is a colorful example of fluorescence in which excitation is induced by UV radiation while de-excitation occurs in the form of visible light.
19.1 ATOMIC SPECTRA

The spectrum of frequencies of electromagnetic radiation emitted or absorbed during transitions of electrons between energy levels within an atom is called atomic spectra. Each element has a characteristic spectrum by which it can be recognized.
All the matter when heated produces light. Solids, liquids, and very dense gases give light with a spectrum showing continuous (not discrete) changes in intensity referred as a continuous spectrum.
A. LINE EMISSION SPECTRUM

The radiations from electrically ‘excited’ gases are discrete rather than continuous (an excited gas gives off only specific frequencies of light). When this light is passed through a spectroscope, a bright-line emission spectrum is observed, containing lines of light of the various frequencies given off by that gas.

Consider an evacuated glass tube filled with a gas (such as helium, neon, mercury or barium) as shown in figure 19.1. If the potential difference is applied to the electrodes, the tube will emit light. If emitted light is passed through aligning slits and then through a spectroscope (such as prism) a series of discrete line is observed, each line corresponds to different wavelength, termed as line emission spectrum. Since each element has its unique set of lines, therefore spectrum can be used to identify a substance.
B. LINE ABSORPTION SPECTRUM

If a beam of white light passes through a sample of the substance. Photons absorbed by the atoms are missing from the transmitted light, causing dark lines (gaps) to appear in the continuous spectrum called line absorption spectrum.

19.3 BOHR MODEL OF HYDROGEN ATOM

Following Rutherford’s proposal that the mass and positive charge are concentrated in a very small region at the center of the atom, the Danish physicist Niels Bohr in 1913 suggested that the atom resembled planetary system, with the electrons circulating about the nucleus like planets orbiting the Sun.

Classical physics requires that an accelerated electric charge, such as orbiting electron, must continuously radiate electromagnetic energy. As it radiates this energy, its total energy would decrease, the electron would spiral in toward the nucleus, and the atom would collapse as shown in figure 19.5. To overcome this difficulty, Bohr proposed that there are certain special states of motion, called stationary states, in which the electron may exist without radiating electromagnetic energy.

In these states, the angular momentum ‘L’ of the electron takes values that are integral multiples of ‘h’. In stationary states, the angular momentum of the electron may have magnitude only of h, 2h, 3h, . . . , but never such values as 2.5h or 3.1h. This is called the quantization of angular momentum.
Bohr Model is Based on the following Postulates

Postulate 1: The electron moves around the nucleus in a circular orbit. The centripetal force required to keep the electron in the circular orbit is provided by the coulomb force between the positively charged nucleus and negatively charged electron. Mathematically
F_centripetal = F_coulomb   hence   mv²/r = k e²/r²        —①

C. HYDROGEN EMISSION SPECTRUM

According to Bohr’s theory the emission line spectrum of an element tells us that atoms of that element emit photons with only certain specific frequencies ‘f’ and hence certain specific energies ‘E = hf’. During the emission of a photon, the internal energy of the atom changes by an amount equal to the energy of the photon.

Each atom has a set of possible energy levels. An atom can have an amount of internal energy equal to any one of these levels, but it cannot have an energy intermediate between two levels. All isolated atoms of a given element have the same set of energy levels, but atoms of different elements have different sets.

Hence 12.1 eV energy is required for an electron to jump from ground state (n =1) to allowed state ( n= 3) in hydrogen atom.
The potential difference required to move an electron from its ground state (n = 1) to the excited state (n = 2, 3, 4, ...) is called excitation potential.

The excitation energy required to move an electron must be equal to the excitation potential. Therefore the first and second excitation potential for hydrogen atom are 10.2 eV and 12.1 eV respectively.
The minimum energy required to remove an electron from the atom in its ground state (n = 1) is called ionization energy.

When an atom absorbs sufficient amount of energy an atom may be raised to a level of n = ∞. The electron then become free from the attractive force of the nucleus. hence   E∞ − E₁ = 0 + E_0
Thus ionization energy for hydrogen atom is 13.6 eV. This means that ionization energy of an atom is numerically equivalent to ground state energy of an atom.
The minimum potential difference required to remove an electron from the atom in its ground state (n= 1) is called ionization potential.
The ionization energy required to remove an electron from an atom must be equal to the ionization potential. Therefore ionization potential for hydrogen atom is also 13.6 eV.

title: Absorption spectra, Balmer wavelengths and de Broglie waves

paragraphs: The lowest energy level is called the ground state, to distinguish it from the higher levels, which are called excited states.

The various lines in the hydrogen atom spectrum are produced when electrons change from higher to lower energy levels and photons are emitted. Electrons can also make transitions in the reverse direction, from lower to higher levels. In this case, an atom absorbs a photon that has precisely the energy needed to produce the transition. Thus, if photons with a continuous range of wavelengths pass through a gas and then are analyzed with a grating spectroscope, a series of dark absorption lines appears in the continuous spectrum. Thus the dark lines indicate the wavelengths removed by the absorption process.

EXAMPLE 19.1 — BALMER SERIES — The Balmer series for hydrogen atom corresponds to electronic transitions that terminate in the state of quantum number n = 2. Find the (a) shortest and (b) longest wavelength of photon emitted in the Balmer’s series of hydrogen atom?

(a) For short wavelength the general formula can be written as
1/λ_S = R_H (1/p² − 1/n_S²)   Putting values   1/λ_S = 1.0974 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ (1/(2)² − 1/(∞)²)
therefore   λ_S = 364.5×10⁻⁹ m = 654.5 nm   Answer

1/λ_L = R_H (1/p² − 1/n_L²)   Putting values   1/λ_L = 1.0974 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ (1/(2)² − 1/(3)²)
therefore   λ_L = 656.09×10⁻⁹ m = 656.1nm   Answer

Find the (a) shortest and (b) longest wavelength of photon emitted in the Layman’s series of hydrogen atom? [Answer: (a) 91 nm, (b) 121.5 nm]
ASSIGNMENT 19.2 — PASCHEN SERIES — What is the wavelength of the second line of paschen series? (Answer: 1281.43 nm)
19.4 DE-BROGLIE WAVES AND HYDROGEN ATOM

Of all the postulates of Bohr Model of the hydrogen atom, the most puzzling is the assumption about the angular momentum that an electron cannot revolve around the nucleus in any arbitrary circular orbit. Only those orbits are possible for which the angular momentum is the integral multiple of h/2π.
In 1923, ten years after Bohr’s work, de Broglie pointed out that his own theory for the wavelength of a moving particle could provide an answer to this question.

19.5 X-RAYS
X-rays are electromagnetic waves with wavelengths in the region of an Angstrom Å (10⁻¹⁰ m).
A. PRODUCTION OF X-RAYS

Figure 19.10 shows an arrangement of producing X-rays. An X-ray tube is a vacuum tube that produces X-rays. It consist of filament heated by current supplied from battery, which emits electrons. These electrons are accelerated towards rotating anode, anode is rotated to reduce overheating. A high voltage power source, for example 30 to 150 kilovolts (kV), is connected across cathode and anode to accelerate the electrons. When such high energy electrons are suddenly stopped by target, an intense beam of X-rays are produced. The X-ray spectrum depends on the anode material and the accelerating voltage. The range of photon energies emitted by the system can be adjusted by changing the applied voltage, and installing aluminum filters of varying thicknesses.

title: X-ray discovery, spectra and characteristic lines
sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf
paragraphs: For your information — X-RAYS DISCOVERY

Röntgen discovered X-rays in November 1895 in his laboratory at the University of Wurzburg, Germany. Röntgen was investigating cathode rays using a fluorescent screen painted with barium platinocyanide and a Crookes tube which he had wrapped in black cardboard. He noticed that when the tube was switched on some invisible rays coming from it were passing through the cardboard to make the screen glow which was placed about 1 meter away.
Röntgen studied them throughly and investigated nearly all the properties associated with them. He is also gave them the name “X-rays” (signifying an unknown quantity).
Wilhelm Conrad Rontgen (Germany). In recognition of the extraordinary services he has rendered by the discovery of X rays he was awarded with Nobel Prize for Physics in 1901

It should be noted that about 1% of the energy generated is emitted/radiated, usually perpendicular to the path of the electron beam, as X-rays, the rest is converted into heat. The target becomes very hot and therefore should have high melting point. Typical target materials are a tungsten-rhenium target on a molybdenum core.
B. X-RAY SPECTRUM
We can understand X-rays by studying the spectrum of radiation emitted. It consist of two parts i.e. characteristic X-rays and continuous X-rays.

A typical example of X-ray spectrum is shown in the figure 19.11. If we look at the spectrum of wavelengths emitted by an X-ray tube, we see that the spectrum consists of two parts: one is series of peaks (K_α, K_β, .... ); characteristic X-rays and the second is Bremsstrahlung; continuous X-rays with a cutoff wavelength λ_o.
C. CHARACTERISTIC OR INNER SHELL TRANSITION X-RAYS

In atoms having many electrons (like molybdenum target in X-ray tube), the electrons are arranged in different orbitals or shells as K, L, M … . When an incoming beam of electrons strike the atom it may remove an inner shell electron from the atom (such as ejecting a K-shell electron). Now an electron from K, L, M shell will rapidly make a transition to fill that vacancy, emitting an X-ray photon in the process. Thus we can explain these characteristic X-rays (the peaks in Figure 19.11) as photons emitted when an electron in an upper state drops down to fill the lower state.

The K lines; K_α, K_β, .... result from transitions into the K shell from L, M, .... shells respectively. Whereas L lines; L_α, L_β, .... result from transitions into the L shell from M, N, .... shells respectively as shown in figure 19.12.
In a similar manner, we label the other X-ray series by M,N, and so forth.

paragraphs: D. CONTINUOUS X-RAYS

An electron by interaction with atoms of the target slows down and thus emits radiation, and in this case it is called bremsstrahlung (German for “braking radiation”) as shown in figure 19.13. Because energy is conserved, the energy of the emitted photon hf, equals the loss of kinetic energy of the electron as
KE − KE′ = hf        —①

An electron may lose all or a part of its energy in such a collision. Since different electrons are slowed down differently in target and thus varying amounts of energies are lost by the electrons in the form of X-rays. Therefore the spectrum obtained is continuous X-ray spectrum. The shortest-wavelength X-ray (the highest frequency) must be due to an electron that gives up all its kinetic energy to produce one photon in a single collision. Since the initial kinetic energy of an electron is equal to the energy given it by the accelerating voltage, V, then
KE = q_eV        —②
In a single collision in which the electron is brought to rest   KE′ = 0        —③
putting values from equation 2 and equation 3 in equation 1
q_eV − 0 = hf   or   q_eV = hf   since   f = c/λ
therefore   q_eV = h c/λ   hence   λ = hc/(q_eV)        (19.9)
The equation 19.9 agrees with experimentally observed values. This result is further evidence that X-rays are a form of electromagnetic radiation (light) and that the photon theory of light is valid.
E. APPLICATIONS OF X-RAYS
The important practical applications of X-rays can be divided into three categories

A. Scientific Applications: The diffraction pattern of X-rays by different crystals give information about internal structure of crystals. The spacing and dispositions of the atoms of crystals can be determined.

B. Industrial Applications: X-rays penetrating ability can be used to detect defects in Rial roads, bridges and large machinery. The structure of rubber and plastics can be analyzed. It is also used at airports to check customers and baggage and by art historians to see if a picture has been painted on top of an older one.

C. Medical Applications: Since bore is more opaque to X-rays than flesh, therefore if X-rays are allowed to pass through the human body a shadow of bone can be obtained on photographic film. The X-ray film reveal the fractures of bones and presence of foreign bodies.

For your information — CT SCANNER
The acronym CAT stands for Computerized Axial Tomography or in short CT (Computerized Tomography).

In CT scan machine there are large number of X-ray detectors. The source and detectors are arranged on a large ring shape structure. In this technique a number of X-ray beams pass simultaneously through the patient. The source and detector are rotated to get views from different directions. Large number of images are obtained and are combined by a computer to get detailed 3D images of the patient. In effect, the CAT scanning technique makes it possible to take an X-ray picture of a cross-sectional ‘slice’ that is perpendicular to the body’s long axis.

EXAMPLE 19.2 — CUTOFF WAVELENGTH — A tungsten target is struck by electrons that have been accelerated from rest through a 40.0-kV potential difference. Find the shortest wavelength of the radiation emitted.

GIVEN — Applied voltage ‘V’ = 40.0-kV = 40.0 × 10³ V; Plank’s constant ‘h’ = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ Js; charge on electron ‘q_e’ = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; speed of light ‘c’ = 3 × 10⁸ ms⁻¹. REQUIRED — Shortest wavelength ‘λ’ = ?

SOLUTION — For electrons accelerated through a potential difference of 40.0 kV, starting from rest, the kinetic energy is KE = e(ΔV) = e(40.0 kV) = 40.0 keV. When these electrons strike the tungsten target, the shortest wavelength possible is produced when the electron loses all its kinetic energy and is brought to rest in a single collision, producing a single photon. The wavelength of the photon produced is
λ_min = hc/(q_eV)
Putting values   λ_min = (6.626×10⁻³⁴ J s × 3 × 10⁸ ms⁻¹) / (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C × 40.0 × 10³ V)
therefore   λ_min = 3.11×10⁻¹¹ m = 0.0311nm   Answer

19.6 LASER

A LASER is a device that emits light through a process of optical amplification based on the stimulated emission of electromagnetic radiation. Intense, monochromatic and coherent beam of light is emitted from LASER source.

The term LASER is abbreviation of Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. Light denotes electromagnetic radiation of any frequency, not only visible light. Therefore LASER operating at microwaves and radio-frequency is called MASER.
To understand how a laser works the terms stimulated emission and population inversion must be understood first.

title: Atomic emission processes and laser action
sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf
paragraphs: A. SPONTANEOUS AND STIMULATED EMISSIONS
There are three means by which radiation can interact with the energy levels of atoms.
i. Spontaneous emission: In the first kind of interaction, an atom in an excited state makes a transition to a lower state, with the emission of a photon.
atom* → atom + photon
where the asterisk (*) indicates an excited state.

ii. Induced Absorption: The second interaction, induced absorption, is responsible for absorption spectra and resonance absorption. An atom in the ground state absorbs a photon (of the proper energy) and makes a transition to an excited state.
atom + photon → atom*

iii. Stimulated emission: The third interaction, which is responsible for the operation of the laser, is stimulated (or induced) emission. In this process, an atom is initially in an excited state. A passing photon of just the right energy (again, equal to the energy difference of the two levels) induces the atom to emit a photon and make a transition to the lower or ground state.
atom* + photon → atom + 2 photon
The two photons that emerge are travel in exactly the same direction with same energy, and the associated electromagnetic waves are perfectly in phase (coherent).
B. LASER ACTION

Suppose we have collection of atoms and potential difference is applied to excite the atoms to the same energy level as shown in figure 19.15. These atoms are confined in a cylinder one side of which is having a totally reflecting mirror and the other is partially reflecting to allow the beam of light to escape.

A photon passes the first atom, causing induced emission and resulting in two photons. This process continues, doubling the number of photons at each step, until building up an intense beam of photons, all coherent and moving in the same direction is emitted from partially reflecting mirror.
However there are few difficulties with this model.

First, it is difficult to keep a collection of atoms in their excited states until they are stimulated to emit the photon. Secondly all the atoms must be in the same excited sate otherwise atoms that happen to be in their ground state undergo absorption and thus remove photons from the beam as it builds up.
These problems can be solved by considering the following situations.
C. META-STABLE STATE
The excited states in atom in which electrons stays for slightly longer period of time before spontaneously falling to ground state are called meta-stable states.

title: Metastable states, population inversion and helium-neon laser pumping
sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf
paragraphs: The excited state decays very rapidly (about 10⁻⁸ s by spontaneous emission) to a lower excited state. Meta-stable state is the state in which the electrons stay for longer duration (about 10⁻³ s). These states make the stimulated emission possible as more time is provided to photons to pass atoms in meta-stable state.
D. POPULATION INVERSION
In a collection of atoms, when there are more atoms in the excited state than in the ground state is called population inversion as shown in figure 19.16.

This is called an “inversion” because under normal conditions at thermal equilibrium, the lower state always has the greater population. The ‘inversion’ is thus an unnatural situation that must be achieved by artificial means, because it is essential for the operation of the laser.
For your information — LASER ALTIMETER.

Figure shows an impressive example of how a laser can be used to measure distances accurately. The photograph in the figure is a three-dimensional map of the Martian topography that was obtained by the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) on the Mars Global Surveyor spacecraft. The map was constructed from 27 million height measurements, each made by sending laser pulses to the Martian surface and measuring their return times.
E. LASER PUMPING

The act of energy transfer from an external source, producing excited states in its atoms is called Laser pumping. The pump energy is usually provided in the form of light (optical pumping) or electric current (electrical pumping).

Let us consider a material whose atoms can reside in four different states. The ground state E_o, two excited states with short life times E₁ and E₃ and meta-stable excited state with long life time E₂ as shown in figure 19.17. When laser pumping is provided atoms are excited to different energy levels, The atoms excited to meta-stable state will stay there longer and after 10⁻⁸ s, electrons in excited state E₃ will jump to meta-stable state E₂, this increase the number of atoms in meta-stable state E₂ with respect to ground state E_o. Thus population inversion is achieved.
F. HELIUM NEON LASER

It is the most common type of gas Laser. A tube with partially reflecting mirrors is filled with helium 85 % and neon 15%. The neon is the lasing or active medium in this tube. Helium and Neon have identical meta-stable states located at 20.61eV and 20.66 eV respectively. The high voltage electric discharge excites the electrons in some of the helium atoms to 20.61 eV meta-stable state.

G. LASER AND ORDINARY LIGHT

Laser light, like the light from an ordinary lightbulb, is emitted when atoms make a transition from higher quantum state to a lower one. However, in a lightbulb the emissions are random, both in time and direction, and in a laser they are coordinated so that the emissions are at the same time and in the same direction.
i. Laser light is highly monochromatic. Light from an ordinary incandescent lightbulb is spread over a continuous range of wavelengths and is not monochromatic.

ii. Laser light is highly coherent. Individual long waves (wave trains) for laser light can be several hundred kilometers long. When two separated beams that have traveled such distances over separate paths are recombined, they are able to form a pattern of interference fringes.

iii. Laser light is highly directional. A laser beam spreads very little; it departs from strict parallelism only because of diffraction at the exit aperture of the laser. Whereas ordinary light spreads.
iv Laser light can be sharply focused. Laser light can be focused to the smaller spot with greater intensity (power per unit area) at that spot as compared to ordinary light.
H. APPLICATIONS OF LASER
Lasers have wide applications some of them are listed below.
i. Lasers in the Medical Field: Lasers have perhaps found the most beneficial and useful applications in the field of medicine. These uses include eye surgery, ulcer removal and disease prevention.

ii. Compact Disks (CDs): Compact disks have digital information (video, music) stored on them, which is read inside the CD player, thus enabling you to hear music. All CD players contain a tiny laser, the job of which is to read the digital codes of information and translate them into music.

iv. Other Uses: Laser fiber optics used by computers and the internet for transferring information and data. Science Tidbits — HOLOGRAPHY

Holography is a method of using interference to record both the phase and intensity of an object and therefore use it to reproduce an accurate 3-dimensional representation of that object. There is a wide variety of holography techniques, but all of them follow the same primary process where holography lasers are split into two different beams and one is directed to the recording media and the other is directed toward the object.

When the scattered light interferes with the reference beam at the recording media, the resultant interference pattern contains both the phase and amplitude of the object. Therefore we do not get just illusion of depth but we generate truly three-dimensional images.
KEY POINTS
Spectrum: The separation of electromagnetic radiation into its component colors or wavelengths
Rydberg formula: The general mathematical form for wavelengths of spectral lines, which is given as
1/λ_n = R_H (1/p² − 1/n²)
Rydberg constant: R_H = 1.0974 × 10⁷ m⁻¹
Postulates of Bohr’s model of H -atom: Three postulates are
⊙ An electron bound to the nucleus in an atom, can move around the nucleus in certain circular orbits without radiating. These orbits are called the discrete stationary states of the atom.
⊙ Only those stationary states are allowed for which orbital angular momentum is, equal to an integral multiple of ‘h’ i.e, mvr = nh/2π
⊙ Whenever an electron makes a transition, i.e, jumps from high energy state E_n to a lower energy state E_p, a photon of energy hf is emitted such that E_n-E_p = hf
Characteristics X-rays: The X-rays emitted in inner shell transition
Continuous X-rays: The X-rays that are emitted in all directions and with a continuous range of frequencies
LASER: Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation.
Stimulated or Induced emission: When the incident photon of energy hf = E_f - E_i induce the atom to decay by emitting a photon that travels in the direction of the incident photon
Population inversion: In a collection of atoms, when there are more atoms in the excited state than in the ground state
Meta-stable state: The excited states in atom in which electrons stays for slightly longer period of time before spontaneously falling to ground state
Laser pumping: The act of energy transfer from an external source, producing excited states in its atoms
